## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Web accessibility patterns as DESIGN-TIME decisions, not code fixes. Narrow scope — four tightly related topics only. (1) The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG): which of its patterns encode decisions a designer makes rather than a developer — specifically disclosure vs accordion vs tabs, dialog vs alertdialog, combobox vs listbox vs select, menu vs menubar vs toolbar, and treegrid vs grid vs table — and what visual and interaction commitments each pattern obliges once chosen (expected keyboard model, focus behavior, visible state). (2) The "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA" rule from the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices and the five rules of ARIA use — concrete named cases where ARIA is the WRONG answer and a native element or a layout change is correct instead, and the specific measured harm bad ARIA causes to screen reader users; cite WebAIM Million data on ARIA correlating with higher detected error rates if it exists. (3) Focus management on route change and view transitions in single-page applications — what the accepted correct behavior is when a route changes, where focus should go, the role of a skip link and a page-title announcement, how the View Transitions API interacts with focus and with prefers-reduced-motion, and the known failure of focus being lost to document body. (4) Live regions and aria-live for asynchronous results — aria-live polite vs assertive, role=status vs role=alert, aria-atomic and aria-relevant, the requirement that the live region exist in the DOM before content is injected, and documented cross-screen-reader failure modes across NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver. Prioritize primary and authoritative sources only: w3.org WAI ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, W3C ARIA specification, WebAIM articles and the WebAIM Million report, and TPGi or Deque technical writeups where W3C is silent. Reject generic blog restatements.

17 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] The APG treats disclosure and accordion as two separate named patterns distinguished by content structure — a disclosure governs a single collapsible/expandable region, while an accordion is a vertically stacked SET of interactive headings each owning a section — so choosing between them is a decision about how many sections exist and whether they are headed, not an implementation detail.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/ (primary)
Quote: "A disclosure is a widget that enables content to be either collapsed (hidden) or expanded (visible). ... An accordion is a vertically stacked set of interactive headings that each contain a title, content snippet, or thumbnail representing a section of content."
Verifier evidence (high): VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCE (fetched live 2026-08-01, not from memory).

1. Two separate named patterns — CONFIRMED. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/ lists them as distinct entries with distinct pattern pages: "Accordion (Sections With Show/Hide Functionality)" and "Disclosure (Show/Hide)". Both /patterns/accordion/ and /patterns/disclosure/ resolve to separate full pattern pages (keyboard, ARIA, examples). Notably, curl of each page shows ZERO occurrences of the other pattern's name — they do not cross-reference at all, which strengthens rather than weakens "separate named patterns."

2. Supporting quote is verbatim-accurate. Disclosure page: "A disclosure is a widget that enables content to be either collapsed (hidden) or expanded (visible). It has two elements: a disclosure button and a section of content whose visibility is controlled by the button." Accordion page: "An accordion is a vertically stacked set of interactive headings that each contain a title, content snippet, or thumbnail representing a section of content." Plus accordion terminology: "Accordion Panel: Section of content associated with an accordion header." So "single region" vs "stacked set of headings each owning a section" is APG's own language, not a gloss.

3. "Whether they are headed" is a real, normative APG-encoded difference. Accordion's ARIA section mandates: "Each accordion header button is wrapped in an element with role heading that has a value set for aria-level that is appropriate for the information architecture of the page... The button element is the only element inside the heading element." The Disclosure pattern's ARIA section has NO heading requirement — only role=button, aria-expanded, optional aria-controls. That is an information-architecture (design-time) commitment, supporting the claim's framing.

QUALIFICATION (accuracy note, not a refutation): the claim's first conjunct — "how many sections exist" — is NOT a clean discriminator on its own. APG's own disclosure example https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/disclosure/examples/disclosure-faq/ says: "The following example demonstrates using the Disclosure Pattern to create a SET of frequently asked questions where the answers may be independently shown or hidden" — 4+ collapsible sections, markup is <li><button aria-expanded>, no heading wrappers. So multiplicity alone does not make an accordion. The claim survives because it states the criteria conjunctively ("how many sections exist AND whether they are headed"), and the unheaded multi-item FAQ correctly resolves to disclosure under that conjunction. Anyone restating this should lead with headedness/grouping, not section count.

CONTESTED-BOUNDARY EVIDENCE FOUND (disclosed for honesty): w3c/aria-practices issue #2445 "Why is the Disclosure FAQ widget not an Accordion?" is open with no editor answer — the boundary is questioned even inside W3C. Third-party guidance conflicts on the count criterion: NZ Government web-a11y guidance defines an accordion as "a collection of 2 or more disclosures one after the other," which contradicts APG's own FAQ example. This qualifies the claim's precision but does not contradict its core assertion, which is only that APG names and defines them as two patterns distinguished by content structure.

Source quality matches claim strength: w3.org APG is the primary source for a claim about what the APG says; claim is current (pages fetched today); not marketing, not a benchmark, not forum speculation.

### [1] The APG separates grid from table on the basis of interactivity and keyboard navigation, not visual appearance: a grid is defined by directional-key navigation (arrows, Home, End) among its contents, whereas an ARIA table is explicitly declared static and 'not an interactive widget' — so picking 'grid' commits the design to an arrow-key navigation model.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/ (primary)
Quote: "A grid widget is a container that enables users to navigate the information or interactive elements it contains using directional navigation keys, such as arrow keys, Home, and End. ... Like an HTML table element, a WAI-ARIA table is a static tabular structure containing one or more rows that each contain one or more cells; it is not an interactive widget."
Verifier evidence (high): Both quotes verified VERBATIM by fetching the raw HTML of the primary sources (not just a summarizer).

1) APG Grid pattern (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/), "About This Pattern", exact text: "A grid widget is a container that enables users to navigate the information or interactive elements it contains using directional navigation keys, such as arrow keys, Home, and End."

2) APG Table pattern (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/table/), exact text: "Like an HTML table element, a WAI-ARIA table is a static tabular structure containing one or more rows that each contain one or more cells; it is not an interactive widget. Thus, its cells are not focusable or selectable."

3) The "not visual appearance" half of the claim is directly stated on the same APG grid page: "using the grid role on an element does not necessarily imply that its visual presentation is tabular." The page then frames the grid-vs-table choice explicitly in interaction terms: "A grid is a composite widget so it: Always contains multiple focusable elements. Only one of the focusable elements contained by the grid is included in the page tab sequence. Requires the author to provide code that manages focus movement inside it. All focusable elements contained in a table are included in the page tab sequence." Table pattern's Keyboard Interaction section is "Not applicable."

4) Corroborated by the NORMATIVE spec (grepped from https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/): role grid = "A composite widget containing a collection of one or more rows with one or more cells where some or all cells in the grid are focusable by using methods of two-dimensional navigation, such as directional arrow keys." role table = "The table role is intended for tabular containers which are not interactive. If the tabular container maintains a selection state, provides its own two-dimensional navigation, or allows the user to rearrange or otherwise manipulate its contents ... authors SHOULD use grid or treegrid instead."

Counter-evidence search found no dispute — the leading critical voices AGREE with the claim's substance and only warn against overusing grid: Adrian Roselli, "ARIA Grid As an Anti-Pattern" and "Don't Turn a Table into an ARIA Grid Just for a Clickable Row"; Sarah Higley, "Grids Part 1/2". Their position (grid only when spreadsheet-style cell-by-cell keyboard navigation is a real requirement) reinforces rather than contradicts "picking grid commits the design to an arrow-key navigation model."

Two minor caveats, neither refuting: (a) the cited URL is the APG patterns INDEX; the verbatim text lives on the child pages /patterns/grid/ and /patterns/table/ — a citation-precision nit, not a sourcing failure. (b) The normative spec's trigger for grid is slightly BROADER than arrow keys alone (selection state, or rearranging/manipulating contents also warrant grid), so "a grid is defined by directional-key navigation" is APG's framing and is marginally narrower than ARIA 1.2 — it understates rather than overstates. Currency: APG is a living W3C document, ARIA 1.2 is a W3C Recommendation, both current as of the check.

### [2] Treegrid is a third, distinct pattern from grid and table, defined by hierarchy plus editability/interactivity of tabular information — meaning the design-time question separating it from grid is whether rows nest and expand, not how the data is styled.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/ (primary)
Quote: "A treegrid widget presents a hierarchical data grid consisting of tabular information that is editable or interactive."
Verifier evidence (high): Tried to refute; all three primary sources corroborate.

1) Quote accuracy + "third distinct pattern": the APG patterns index (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) lists Table, Grid and Treegrid as three separate patterns with distinct pages. Verbatim index descriptions: Table — "Like an HTML table element, a WAI-ARIA table is a static tabular structure containing one or more rows that each contain one or more cells; it is not an interactive widget."; Grid — "A grid widget is a container that enables users to navigate the information or interactive elements it contains using directional navigation keys, such as arrow keys, Home, and End."; Treegrid — "A treegrid widget presents a hierarchical data grid consisting of tabular information that is editable or interactive." The supporting quote is verbatim and not truncated in a way that changes meaning.

2) Hierarchy, not styling, is the separator — corroborated independently by the ARIA spec (https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#treegrid): treegrid = "A grid whose rows can be expanded and collapsed in the same manner as for a tree", Superclass Roles: grid, tree. The APG treegrid page adds: "any row in the hierarchy may have child rows, and rows with children may be expanded or collapsed to show or hide the children", with aria-expanded on parent rows and Right Arrow "If focus is on a collapsed row, expands the row." / Left Arrow "If focus is on an expanded row, collapses the row."

3) Negative check on the Grid pattern page (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/): it contains no mention of hierarchy, expandable/collapsible rows, aria-expanded, or treegrid. It scopes grid to "presenting tabular information (data grids) and grouping other widgets (layout grids)." So nothing in the grid pattern competes for the nesting case.

4) Searched for contradiction. MDN's treegrid role page states the operative design-time rule even more explicitly: use treegrid, not grid, when rows need aria-expanded (or aria-posinset/aria-setsize/aria-level). Sarah Higley's "Grids Part 2: Semantics" (sarahmhigley.com) reinforces rather than contradicts: aria-level and aria-expanded are "only supported on rows within treegrids, and are not supported in either grids or tables." No credible source found asserting styling or visual density determines the role choice.

Two qualifications that do NOT refute the claim but should ride with it: (a) taxonomically treegrid is a *subclass* of grid and tree, so "third, distinct pattern" is true at the APG pattern level but is a specialization, not an orthogonal third thing; (b) the distinction is also gated on interactivity — hierarchy alone is insufficient, since static hierarchical data belongs in a table, not a treegrid (APG treegrid requires editable/interactive content and requires every cell be focusable: screen reader users in application mode "hear only focusable elements and content that labels focusable elements"). Real-world AT support for composite grid/treegrid widgets is documented as uneven, but that is an implementation caveat, not a challenge to the design-time separation.

### [3] Choosing the combobox pattern does not settle the interaction — the designer must additionally choose a popup type, which the APG restricts to exactly four roles (listbox, tree, grid, or dialog), each carrying its own keyboard and structural obligations.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/ (primary)
Quote: "The popup is an element that has role listbox, tree, grid, or dialog."
Verifier evidence (high): Attempted refutation on all five checklist axes; none landed.

1) Quote-to-claim fit: verified verbatim on the primary source. WebFetch of https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/ returns "The popup is an element that has role listbox, tree, grid, or dialog." — exactly four roles, closed list, no "such as" or "for example" hedge. The claim's "exactly four" is not an overreach.

2) Stronger backing than the claim asserts: the restriction is not merely APG guidance (APG is non-normative). W3C ARIA issue w3c/aria#2132 (closed, resolved via PR #2134) quotes the normative spec text: "Authors MUST ensure the popup element associated with a combobox has a role of listbox, tree, grid, or dialog." The issue was an editorial clarification of overlapping paragraphs, NOT a dispute of the four-role list. So the claim is if anything understated.

3) "Each carrying its own keyboard and structural obligations" — confirmed directly from the APG combobox keyboard tables, which are branched by popup type:
 - listbox: Down Arrow "Moves focus to and selects the next option"; structure = option + aria-selected.
 - grid: Down Arrow "Moves focus one cell down"; Right/Left "Moves focus one cell to the right/left. Optionally, if focus is on the right-most/left-most cell in the row, focus may move to the first/last cell in the following/previous row"; structure = gridcell/rows.
 - tree: Right Arrow "When focus is on a closed node, opens the node; focus and selection do not move. When focus is on an open node, moves focus to the first child node"; structure = treeitem, "some or all parent nodes may not be selectable values."
 - dialog: "Unlike other combobox popups, dialogs do not support aria-activedescendant so DOM focus moves into the dialog from the combobox" — i.e. a different focus model entirely, not just different arrow keys.
 This is a real, documented per-popup divergence in both keyboard model and required child roles.

4) Corroboration + a genuine exclusion: aria-haspopup is implicitly listbox for combobox; if the popup is anything else, aria-haspopup must be tree, grid, or dialog. Notably aria-haspopup="menu" — a valid value for the attribute generally — is NOT valid for a combobox popup, which confirms the list is exclusive rather than illustrative (MDN combobox role / aria-haspopup pages agree with W3C here).

5) Currency and source type: ARIA 1.2 / current APG, checked live August 2026; the only relevant spec churn (#2132/#2134) is editorial and tightened the same wording. Source is w3.org primary, not a blog restatement, not marketing, not a benchmark.

Only caveat worth flagging to the parent (does not refute): the "designer must choose" framing is the research question's own design-time lens, not language W3C uses — APG addresses authors/developers. The factual core (four roles, each with distinct keyboard/structural commitments) is exactly what the primary source says.

### [4] The open/closed state of the popup must be exposed programmatically via aria-expanded on the combobox element, mirroring the visible state — so the visual expand/collapse affordance in a design is a binding accessibility commitment, not decoration.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/ (primary)
Quote: "When the combobox popup is not visible, the element with role combobox has aria-expanded set to false. When the popup element is visible, aria-expanded is set to true."
Verifier evidence (high): Attempted refutation on all five checklist axes; claim survives.

1) QUOTE FIDELITY — verified verbatim at source. WebFetch of https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/ returns exactly: "When the combobox popup is not visible, the element with role combobox has aria-expanded set to false." / "When the popup element is visible, aria-expanded is set to true." / "Note that elements with role combobox have a default value for aria-expanded of false." The quote is not fabricated, not truncated, and the attribute is placed on the element with role=combobox — exactly as the claim states.

2) STRENGTH OF "MUST" — the APG is explicitly non-normative, so I tried to kill the modal "must" by showing the APG only advises. It fails: aria-expanded is a REQUIRED state for role=combobox in the normative ARIA specification itself (WAI-ARIA 1.2 required states/properties for combobox = aria-expanded, plus aria-controls; ARIA 1.3 dropped aria-controls but kept aria-expanded required). Corroborated by MDN's combobox role reference: "A WAI-ARIA combobox requires only one attribute: aria-expanded... The combobox is in the expanded state when both the combobox element showing its current value and its associated popup element are visible. When expanded, aria-expanded='true' must be set." Two independent sources (W3C normative spec + MDN) back the "must", so the claim is not resting on a non-normative guide alone.

3) CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE — searched w3.org, TPGi, Deque, WebAIM, a11ysupport.io and issue trackers for any source disputing or qualifying the requirement. Found zero sources arguing aria-expanded is optional or wrong on combobox. What exists is AT-side bug reports (nvaccess/nvda #9096 aria-haspopup suppressing state announcement, #8341 ::before content suppressing state change announcement, MUI #34074, UI5 #2392) — these are screen-reader/implementation defects in conveying the state, which presuppose rather than contradict the authoring requirement. No credible source disputes it.

4) CURRENCY — not outdated. The APG page is the live current pattern; the requirement carried forward from ARIA 1.2 into the 1.3 editor's draft (w3c.github.io/aria). Only the legacy ARIA 1.0/1.1 combobox pattern differed (role/aria-expanded on a wrapper div, now deprecated), and the claim cites the current pattern, not the legacy one.

5) NOT MARKETING/FORUM — primary W3C normative + W3C APG + MDN. Source quality exceeds what the claim's strength requires.

QUALIFICATIONS (do not refute, but should be carried into the writeup):
- Scope: the requirement binds the ARIA pattern (role=combobox). A native <select> exposes expanded/collapsed through the platform accessibility API without the author writing aria-expanded — so the designer's expand affordance is only an *authoring* commitment when the design is not implemented with a native control. The claim as worded is silent on this.
- aria-expanded has an implicit default of false on role=combobox, so strictly the collapsed value need not be written; the binding that actually matters is that the true/false value must track popup visibility.
- The second clause ("binding accessibility commitment, not decoration") is the researcher's design-time framing, not source text. It is a fair inference from the normative binding of state to visibility, but it is interpretation, not quotation, and should be presented as such.

### [5] Choosing the ARIA grid pattern over a plain table is a keyboard-model commitment made at design time: a grid is a composite widget that exposes exactly one focusable element to the page tab sequence (roving focus), whereas every focusable element inside a table stays in the tab sequence. The same visual table therefore yields two entirely different keyboard experiences depending on which pattern the designer picks.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/ (primary)
Quote: "A `grid` is a composite widget so it: Always contains multiple focusable elements. Only one of the focusable elements contained by the grid is included in the page tab sequence. … All focusable elements contained in a table are included in the page tab sequence."
Verifier evidence (high): VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCE, NOT REFUTED.

1) Quote is verbatim and current. Fetched https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/ on 2026-08-01. The page opens the comparison with "When presenting content that is tabular, consider the following factors when choosing between implementing this `grid` pattern or the `table` pattern," then lists that a grid "Always contains multiple focusable elements," "Only one of the focusable elements contained by the grid is included in the page tab sequence," and "Requires the author to provide code that manages focus movement inside it," versus "All focusable elements contained in a table are included in the page tab sequence." The supporting quote is not trimmed or reordered in a misleading way.

2) Independently corroborated by two more W3C pages. The APG Table pattern (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/table/) states the same asymmetry from the other side: "Since a table is not a widget, each widget contained in a table is a separate stop in the page tab sequence" and "If the number of widgets is large, replacing the table with a grid can dramatically reduce the length of the page tab sequence because a grid is a composite widget that can contain other widgets." The APG keyboard-interface practice (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/) generalizes it: "the tab sequence should include only one focusable element of a composite UI component. Once a composite contains focus, keys other than Tab and Shift + Tab enable the user to move focus among its focusable elements." Three primary W3C pages, consistent.

3) Adversarial search found the strongest published critic of role=grid — Adrian Roselli, "ARIA Grid As an Anti-Pattern" (2020) and "Don't Turn a Table into an ARIA Grid Just for a Clickable Row" (2023) — and he does NOT dispute the mechanism. He concedes it directly: "If your objective is to reduce tab stops on a page, a grid will do that." His objection is to the wisdom of the choice, not the fact of it, which if anything reinforces the claim's "this is a decision with consequences" framing. No source found that contradicts the tab-sequence behavior itself.

4) Source quality matches claim strength. This is a mechanical, low-extraordinariness claim about documented widget behavior, sourced to the exact W3C page that defines it. Not marketing, not a benchmark, not forum speculation. APG is a living document and the text is present today, so not outdated.

QUALIFICATIONS (do not refute, but should ride along with the claim):
- "(roving focus)" is loose. APG sanctions TWO focus-management techniques for composites — roving tabindex and aria-activedescendant. Under aria-activedescendant the container holds DOM focus and interior cells are not DOM-focusable at all. The single-tab-stop conclusion holds either way, but "roving focus" should not be stated as the only mechanism.
- The "design time" / "the designer picks" attribution is the analyst's framing; W3C consistently says "the author." That framing is defensible — APG itself presents it as a choice made before implementation, with obligations attached — but it is interpretation layered on the source, not a W3C quotation.
- Roselli's perception gap is a material addition, not a contradiction: "as of now `grid` semantics are only exposed to screen reader users. While a screen reader user will hear the `grid` role announcement... a keyboard-only user will have no idea." So the claim's "two entirely different keyboard experiences" is true, but one of the two audiences affected gets no announcement that the model changed. That strengthens the design-time argument (the visual design must signal the model) rather than weakening it.

### [6] Grid navigation keys are mutually exclusive with in-cell widget keys: while arrow keys are moving cell-to-cell they cannot operate a combobox or move an editing caret, so the pattern requires an explicit mode switch — Enter to disable grid navigation and enter the cell's input, Escape to restore grid navigation. Any cell design containing an arrow-key-driven control forces this extra mode on users.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/ (primary)
Quote: "While navigation keys, such as arrow keys, are moving focus from cell to cell, they are not available to do something like operate a combobox or move an editing caret inside of a cell. … Enter: Disables grid navigation and: If the cell contains editable content, places focus in an input field, such as a textbox. … Escape: restores grid navigation."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified directly against the live W3C APG grid pattern page (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/) via WebFetch, and cross-checked with the source GitHub file (w3c/aria-practices/content/patterns/grid/grid-pattern.html) surfaced in search. The supporting quote is verbatim/authentic: "While navigation keys, such as arrow keys, are moving focus from cell to cell, they are not available to do something like operate a combobox or move an editing caret inside of a cell," followed by the Enter (disables grid navigation, focuses input) / Escape (restores grid navigation) mechanism exactly as cited. Critically, the claim's narrower assertion — that this mode switch is specifically triggered by arrow-key-driven in-cell controls — is directly supported by the spec's own triggering conditions: the mode switch is needed when a cell contains (1) editable content, (2) multiple widgets, or (3) 'a widget that utilizes arrow keys in its interaction model, such as a radio group or slider.' The spec explicitly contrasts this with the case where 'a cell contains one widget whose operation does not require arrow keys,' which does NOT require the mode switch — confirming the claim's converse logic (arrow-key widgets = mode switch required; non-arrow-key widgets = no mode switch needed) is accurate, not an overreach. No alternative mechanism is offered by the spec for arrow-key-driven in-cell widgets; the mode switch is presented as the standard/required convention ('Following are common keyboard conventions for disabling and restoring grid navigation functions'), and the spec warns that deviating adds complexity. WebSearch corroborates this is a real, currently-documented, and even externally-criticized characteristic of the pattern (Adrian Roselli's 'ARIA Grid As an Anti-Pattern' critiques the mode-switch/complexity issue, and an NVDA GitHub issue documents real screen-reader mode-switching problems with grid comboboxes), which reinforces rather than contradicts the claim. Source is primary (w3.org APG itself), matching the claim's strength; the pattern is current (active in the maintained aria-practices repo), not outdated.

### [7] Choosing the modal dialog pattern obliges a specific keyboard contract: Tab and Shift+Tab must cycle within the dialog and never move focus outside it, and Escape must close it — a focus trap is a required commitment of the pattern, not an optional enhancement.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/ (primary)
Quote: "Tab: Moves focus to the next tabbable element inside the dialog. If focus is on the last tabbable element inside the dialog, moves focus to the first tabbable element inside the dialog. […] Escape: Closes the dialog. […] Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog. However, unlike most non-modal dialogs, modal dialogs do not provide means for moving keyboard focus outside the dialog window without closing the dialog."
Verifier evidence (high): Direct WebFetch of https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/ confirms the supporting quote is verbatim/accurate: the Keyboard Interaction section lists Tab/Shift+Tab cycling within the dialog (wrapping first↔last tabbable element) and Escape closing the dialog, and explicitly states "Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog," contrasting modal dialogs with non-modal ones which "provide means for moving keyboard focus outside the dialog window without closing the dialog." This is presented in the pattern's normative Keyboard Interaction section (the same section structure APG uses to define what a conforming implementation of a named pattern must do), so characterizing it as an obligatory commitment of the pattern (not an optional add-on) is an accurate paraphrase, not an overreach.

Checked for contradicting evidence via WebSearch. Found Scott O'Hara's "There Is No Need to Trap Focus on a Dialog Element" (CSS-Tricks/personal), a credible accessibility-practitioner critique arguing WCAG itself doesn't normatively require focus-trapping and that native <dialog> + `inert` achieves the same effect without manual JS trap-focus code. This does not refute the claim: it disputes *implementation technique* (hand-rolled JS focus-trap vs. inert-based containment), not the behavioral contract itself — O'Hara's alternative still results in Tab/Shift+Tab being unable to reach content outside the dialog, which is the same keyboard contract the claim describes. It's a critique of how developers achieve containment, not evidence that APG's modal-dialog pattern lacks this requirement or that the requirement is optional within the pattern as documented.

Source quality (primary W3C APG page) matches the claim's strength, content is current (fetched today, matches known/expected APG structure, no deprecation notices), and this is not a marketing/blog restatement — it's a direct primary-source quote correctly scoped to "once chosen, this pattern obliges X."

### [8] The pattern mandates a two-sided focus-transfer rule: focus moves into the dialog on open, and returns to the invoking element on close (unless that element no longer exists) — making focus origin/destination a design-time decision about which control opens the dialog.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/ (primary)
Quote: "When a dialog opens, focus moves to an element inside the dialog. […] When a dialog closes, focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog unless either: The invoking element no longer exists."
Verifier evidence (high): Live-fetched https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/ and confirmed the quote verbatim: "When a dialog opens, focus moves to an element inside the dialog" and "When a dialog closes, focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog unless either: [1] The invoking element no longer exists. Then, focus is set on another element that provides logical work flow. [2] The work flow design includes conditions that can occasionally make focusing a different element a more logical choice..." This directly supports the claim's core assertion of a two-sided focus-transfer rule (in on open, back to invoker on close). The claim's parenthetical "(unless that element no longer exists)" mirrors the excerpt given in the claim itself and omits the second, workflow-design exception category that the full pattern also lists — a minor incompleteness, not a misrepresentation, since the claim doesn't assert exhaustiveness of exceptions. The further inference — that this makes focus origin/destination "a design-time decision about which control opens the dialog" — is a reasonable analytical framing (the invoking control is chosen at design time, and the pattern's rule for return-focus is defined relative to that control) rather than an overreach fabricating APG language it doesn't use. solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

input.caveats: Two of the four requested topics returned zero surviving claims: (1) SPA route-change/View-Transitions-API focus management and (2) live regions/aria-live are entirely unaddressed by verified evidence — treat as "not researched," not as "no such pattern exists." Several plausible claims were explicitly refuted by 3-vote panels and must not be reused even though they sound right: the dialog-vs-alertdialog distinguishing criterion (0-3); combobox's defining criterion vs listbox/select (0-3); combobox virtual-focus/aria-activedescendant claim (0-3); grid's "arrow-key-only navigation is non-negotiable" claim (0-3); grid's "application-mode silently skips content" harm claim (1-2, closest refuted vote); menu submenu aria-haspopup+aria-expanded requirement (0-3); disclosure's "exactly two elements" structural definition (1-2); disclosure's "minimal keyboard model, must be a button not a link" claim (0-3). The disclosure-vs-accordion boundary claim that did survive (2-1) is itself contested — a W3C GitHub issue (aria-practices #2445) is open with no editor resolution, and third-party guidance conflicts with APG's own FAQ example on the "count of sections" criterion. The two dialog focus-contract claims (focus trap, focus transfer) survived only 2-1; Scott O'Hara's published dissent argues focus-trapping isn't strictly normative in WCAG and native <dialog>+inert is a valid alternative — this challenges implementation technique, not the behavioral contract itself. WebAIM Million's ARIA-vs-error-rate figures are explicitly correlational per the source's own framing, not causal. Several verification passes (WebAIM claims, the "role is a promise" claim) had WebSearch budget exhausted and relied on primary-source WebFetch alone rather than cross-source triangulation. No TPGi or Deque source survived verification despite being named as fallback sources, and no claim directly cites the "five rules of ARIA use" document itself.
input.summary: Verified evidence strongly supports treating a specific slice of the APG as design-time commitments rather than developer plumbing: grid-vs-table locks in a roving-tabindex/single-tab-stop keyboard model versus every-widget-tabbable; treegrid adds a hierarchy/expand-collapse contract on top of grid; combobox forces a choice among exactly four popup roles (listbox/tree/grid/dialog) each with distinct keyboard and focus semantics, plus a mandatory aria-expanded state that must mirror visible open/closed state; menu/menubar commits to arrows-navigate/Tab-exits roving focus plus a fixed open→first-item and Escape→return-focus contract; and modal dialog bundles a focus trap, bidirectional focus transfer, content-dependent initial-focus placement, and a conditional aria-modal that only applies when the design truly enforces modality both behaviorally and visually. WebAIM Million (2026) supplies the clearest quantitative backing for "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA": pages with ARIA average 59.1 detected errors versus 42 without (~41% more, scaling with ARIA attribute count), and of the 5.7% of home pages using role="menu", 22% actively introduce barriers from incomplete markup — concrete measured harm from half-implemented patterns, consistent with the APG's own framing that a role is "a promise" carrying no native keyboard behavior. Critically, the adversarial verification process produced zero surviving, source-backed claims on the other two requested topics — SPA route-change/View-Transitions-API focus management, and live regions/aria-live behavior — so this report cannot answer those two topics at all and that gap should be treated as unresearched rather than as evidence of no pattern.

findings.claim: Disclosure vs accordion vs tabs is a content-structure decision, not an implementation detail. A disclosure controls one collapsible region and only requires that its trigger's aria-expanded be kept in sync with visibility (aria-controls is optional wiring, not the required deliverable); an accordion is APG's name for a vertically-stacked SET of interactive headings each owning a section, and headedness/information-architecture is the discriminating signal APG actually encodes in required markup (mandatory heading-wrapped buttons for accordion, no such requirement for disclosure).
findings.evidence: APG: 'A disclosure is a widget that enables content to be either collapsed (hidden) or expanded (visible)... two elements: a disclosure button and a section of content.' vs 'An accordion is a vertically stacked set of interactive headings that each contain a title... representing a section of content,' with a mandatory heading-role wrapper on each accordion button. Disclosure: 'When the content is visible, the element with role button has aria-expanded set to true... Optionally, the element with role button has a value specified for aria-controls.' Downgraded to medium: the boundary claim survived only 2-1 and a W3C issue (aria-practices #2445) is open on exactly this line; a stronger competing claim asserting disclosure = 'exactly two elements' as the structural distinguisher was refuted 1-2, and a claim asserting disclosure's keyboard model (no arrows, must-be-button) was refuted 0-3.

findings.claim: Grid vs table vs treegrid is fundamentally a keyboard-interaction-model and tab-sequence decision, not a visual/styling one. A grid is a composite widget exposing exactly one focusable element to the page tab sequence (arrow keys move within it), while every focusable element in a table stays in the tab sequence and a table is explicitly 'not an interactive widget.' Treegrid is a further specialization requiring hierarchy (expandable/collapsible rows via aria-expanded, Left/Right Arrow to collapse/expand) plus editable/interactive cell content. Any grid cell containing an arrow-key-driven control (combobox, slider, radio group) forces an explicit Enter-to-enter/Escape-to-restore mode switch because navigation arrows and in-widget arrows cannot coexist.
findings.evidence: 'A grid widget is a container that enables users to navigate the information or interactive elements it contains using directional navigation keys... using the grid role does not necessarily imply that its visual presentation is tabular.' 'A WAI-ARIA table is a static tabular structure... it is not an interactive widget.' Grid: 'Only one of the focusable elements contained by the grid is included in the page tab sequence' vs Table: 'All focusable elements contained in a table are included in the page tab sequence.' Treegrid (spec): 'A grid whose rows can be expanded and collapsed in the same manner as for a tree.' Grid mode-switch: 'While navigation keys... are moving focus from cell to cell, they are not available to do something like operate a combobox... Enter: Disables grid navigation... Escape: restores grid navigation.' All four underlying claims unanimous 3-0 across multiple primary W3C pages; a related claim about a specific documented screen-reader harm from grid's application mode was refuted 1-2 and should not be reused.

findings.claim: Combobox forces two separate design-time decisions: which of exactly four popup roles to use (listbox, tree, grid, or dialog — a closed list per the normative spec, not illustrative), each carrying a distinct keyboard model and focus mechanism (e.g. dialog popups move real DOM focus in, unlike the other three which use aria-activedescendant-style patterns); and keeping aria-expanded on the combobox element in sync with the popup's visible open/closed state, which is a required state per the normative ARIA spec, not just APG guidance.
findings.evidence: 'The popup is an element that has role listbox, tree, grid, or dialog' — confirmed as a MUST in normative spec via W3C issue w3c/aria#2132/#2134. Per-popup divergence: listbox 'Down Arrow moves focus to and selects the next option'; grid 'Down Arrow moves focus one cell down'; tree 'Right Arrow... opens the node'; dialog 'Unlike other combobox popups, dialogs do not support aria-activedescendant so DOM focus moves into the dialog.' State sync: 'When the combobox popup is not visible... aria-expanded set to false. When the popup element is visible, aria-expanded is set to true' — required state per ARIA 1.2/1.3, corroborated by MDN. Note: two adjacent claims attempting to name combobox's defining criterion vs listbox/select, and to assert a virtual-focus/aria-activedescendant model as universal to combobox, were both refuted 0-3 — the popup can in fact use real DOM focus (dialog case), so 'virtual focus always' is false.

findings.claim: Choosing the menu/menubar pattern commits the design to a roving-tabindex keyboard model where Tab is NOT the intra-widget navigation key (arrows move between items; Tab enters/exits the whole widget as one stop — incompatible with a plain list of independently-tabbable links or buttons), plus a fixed, non-optional focus-management contract: opening a menu places focus on the first item, and Escape closes the menu and returns focus to the invoking control (menu button or parent menuitem).
findings.evidence: 'Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus among the items in the menu... Each item in the menu has tabindex set to -1, except in a menubar, where the first item has tabindex set to 0.' 'When a menu opens, or when a menubar receives focus, keyboard focus is placed on the first item.' 'Escape: Close the menu that contains focus and return focus to the element or context, e.g., menu button or parent menuitem, from which the menu was opened.' Both claims unanimous 3-0 on the same primary page. A related claim asserting that any submenu-opening item must expose a persistent visible aria-haspopup/aria-expanded affordance (a design-time visual-affordance requirement) was refuted 0-3 and should not be cited.

findings.claim: Choosing the modal dialog pattern (as distinct from a non-modal dialog) obliges a bundled contract: Tab/Shift+Tab must cycle within the dialog and never escape it except via Escape (a focus trap), focus moves in on open and returns to the invoking element on close (unless it no longer exists), initial-focus placement is content-dependent (a static heading/first-paragraph via tabindex=-1 for long/semantic content; the least-destructive action for irreversible operations; the most-frequently-used action otherwise), and aria-modal="true" should only be applied when the design actually enforces modality both behaviorally (no interaction with outside content) and visually (outside content obscured) — because the attribute can hide outside content from assistive technology and a false claim of modality has severe consequences.
findings.evidence: 'Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog... modal dialogs do not provide means for moving keyboard focus outside the dialog window without closing the dialog.' 'When a dialog opens, focus moves to an element inside the dialog... When a dialog closes, focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog unless... the invoking element no longer exists.' Initial focus: 'add tabindex="-1" to a static element at the top of the dialog, such as the dialog title or first paragraph... it may be advisable to set focus on the least destructive action, especially if undoing the action is difficult or impossible.' aria-modal: 'marking a dialog modal by setting aria-modal to true can prevent users of some assistive technologies from perceiving content outside the dialog... mark a dialog modal only when both: Application code prevents all users from interacting... Visual styling obscures the content outside of it.' Downgraded to medium: the focus-trap and focus-transfer sub-claims survived only 2-1 each; a dissenting accessibility practitioner (Scott O'Hara) argues focus-trapping is not strictly a WCAG normative requirement and native <dialog>+inert achieves equivalent containment without hand-rolled trap code — a critique of implementation technique, not of the behavioral contract itself. Separately, a claim attempting to distinguish dialog from alertdialog specifically by communicative intent was refuted 0-3, so no surviving claim in this research differentiates the two roles.

findings.claim: ARIA roles carry no native keyboard behavior or styling — applying a role is, in APG's own words, a 'promise' that the author has separately implemented the expected interaction — which is the underlying reason every pattern above (disclosure, grid, combobox, menu, dialog) encodes a specific required keyboard model rather than being a cosmetic labeling choice.
findings.evidence:
'
Place Order
Is a promise that the author of that div has also incorporated JavaScript that provides the keyboard interactions expected for a button. Unlike HTML input elements, ARIA roles do not cause browsers to provide keyboard behaviors or styling. Using a role without fulfilling the promise of that role is similar to making a "Place Order" button that abandons an order and empties the shopping cart.' Same page states APG's objective is 'to define expected behaviors for each ARIA role,' which matches how every surviving pattern-specific finding above is structured (a distinct Keyboard Interaction section per pattern). This is the closest surviving evidence to the research question's 'five rules of ARIA use' framing, though no claim directly quoting that specific named document survived.

findings.claim: WebAIM Million (2026, ~1,000,000 home pages scanned) gives concrete, measured support for 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA': pages containing ARIA average 59.1 detected accessibility errors versus 42 on pages without ARIA (roughly 41% more), with error count scaling as more ARIA attributes are present; and for one specific named pattern, role="menu" (present on 5.7% of home pages), 22% of those implementations actively introduce accessibility barriers due to missing required ARIA menu markup and keyboard interactions.
findings.evidence: 'Home pages with ARIA present had significantly more errors (59.1 on average) than pages without ARIA (42 on average)... Increased ARIA usage on pages was associated with higher detected errors. The more ARIA attributes that were present, the more detected accessibility errors could be expected.' '5.7% of home pages had an ARIA menu (role="menu"), but 22% of those ARIA menus introduced accessibility barriers due to the lack of necessary ARIA menu markup and interactions.' Both unanimous 3-0 against the primary source explicitly prioritized by the research brief. Caveat carried from the source itself: this is correlational, not a controlled causal test — ARIA-heavy pages also tend to be more complex overall. This is the only surviving evidence addressing topic 2's request for named concrete cases and measured harm; no claim survived naming a specific case where a native element/layout change is the objectively correct substitute for ARIA (the closest candidate — disclosure trigger must be a button, not a link — was refuted 0-3).

findings.claim: No verified evidence survived on either of the two remaining requested topics: (a) focus management on route change / View Transitions API in SPAs — correct focus destination, the role of skip links and page-title announcements, View Transitions API interaction with focus and prefers-reduced-motion, and the known focus-lost-to-body failure; and (b) live regions for async results — aria-live polite vs assertive, role=status vs role=alert, aria-atomic/aria-relevant, the DOM-must-exist-before-injection requirement, and documented NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver failure modes. Zero claims on either topic appear in either the confirmed or refuted lists, indicating this research pass did not produce citable material for them at all.
